stories.headline: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.title: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.summary: Any person, place, organisation or nation would change with time. If the period is 25 years, these changes can be expected to be deeper, wider, profound and fundamental.None of this commonsense anticipation could have prepared India and the world for the distance the country has traversed since Narendra Modi assumed public office for the first time—on October 7, 2001—as Gujarat’s chief minister. To put these momentous changes in perspective and construe what they augur for the future, we sought out some of the best and brightest minds, a select group that has been in the thick of things one way or the other.What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general. But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more. Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story. Sure, it is nothing short of stupendous that India’s economy has grown from $500 billion in 2001 to nearly $4 trillion. But the more interesting story is “how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more”.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsAshishkumar Chauhan, writing for us while still emerging from the demanding process of orchestrating one of the largest IPOs in India’s capital markets history, points out that when Modi took charge as Gujarat’s chief minister for the first time, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake of January that year. “He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one,” says the CEO of the National Stock Exchange of India.What a story it turned out to be! That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally. Modi’s stated philosophy, Chauhan says, is together with all, development for all, trust of all, and effort of all. “In capital markets, at least,” he says, “that has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.”Arundhati Bhattacharya, CEO of Salesforce South Asia, sees it as the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength. The figures, she says, illustrate a distinctive Indian model. “The government helped build common rails and establish trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation,” says Bhattacharya.Pawan Chandana, whose startup Skyroot is soaring on the fuel of the government’s space policies, says the biggest transformation is harder to quantify and describes it as “the expansion of what young Indians believe they can build”.Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, Biocon’s executive chairperson, shares this belief. “The most consequential change,” she says, “has been the emergence of self-belief.”Sunil Kant Munjal, chairman of The Hero Enterprise, describes it as the “permission to think big”. The biggest change of the last quarter century, he says, is not a single policy but the mindset change. “India gave itself permission to think big without losing track of the granular. A significant part of that shift traces back to the man who took charge in Gandhinagar that October, and who has now spent a quarter-century in government,” says Munjal.Pratyush Kumar, Sarvam AI’s co-founder, points out that in 2001, the idea that India could build digital infrastructure for a billion people would have sounded like a distant aspiration. Few countries had attempted anything like it. “What emerged over the next two decades was an unusual consequence, with the state building the foundation on which private enterprise could build at scale,” he says.Sumant Sinha, who calls his renewable energy firm ReNew “a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision”, says the sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Modi has brought have changed the feel of India. The biggest change, for him, is not any individual programme but that prosperity feels more widely distributed. “Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did,” says Sinha.Of course, the job is far from done. Suman Bery, economist and former vice chairman of Niti Aayog, the government’s think tank, says: “It would be fatal to assume that, despite the past record, a steady 6 percent growth is assured. It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible.” In his view, policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital.Shah of Mahindra says the India of 2001 had aspiration and the India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability. “The India of 2047,” he says, “must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.”Bhattacharya of Salesforce says the next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive. “But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.”

body: None of this commonsense anticipation could have prepared India and the world for the distance the country has traversed since Narendra Modi assumed public office for the first time—on October 7, 2001—as Gujarat’s chief minister.

To put these momentous changes in perspective and construe what they augur for the future, we sought out some of the best and brightest minds, a select group that has been in the thick of things one way or the other.

What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general.
But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more.
Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.
Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story.
Sure, it is nothing short of stupendous that India’s economy has grown from $500 billion in 2001 to nearly $4 trillion.
But the more interesting story is “how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more”.

Ashishkumar Chauhan, writing for us while still emerging from the demanding process of orchestrating one of the largest IPOs in India’s capital markets history, points out that when Modi took charge as Gujarat’s chief minister for the first time, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake of January that year.
“He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one,” says the CEO of the National Stock Exchange of India.
What a story it turned out to be!
That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally.
Modi’s stated philosophy, Chauhan says, is together with all, development for all, trust of all, and effort of all.

“In capital markets, at least,” he says, “that has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.” Arundhati Bhattacharya, CEO of Salesforce South Asia, sees it as the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.
The figures, she says, illustrate a distinctive Indian model.
“The government helped build common rails and establish trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility.
The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation,” says Bhattacharya.

Pawan Chandana, whose startup Skyroot is soaring on the fuel of the government’s space policies, says the biggest transformation is harder to quantify and describes it as “the expansion of what young Indians believe they can build”.
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, Biocon’s executive chairperson, shares this belief.
“The most consequential change,” she says, “has been the emergence of self-belief.” Sunil Kant Munjal, chairman of The Hero Enterprise, describes it as the “permission to think big”.
The biggest change of the last quarter century, he says, is not a single policy but the mindset change.
“India gave itself permission to think big without losing track of the granular.
A significant part of that shift traces back to the man who took charge in Gandhinagar that October, and who has now spent a quarter-century in government,” says Munjal.
Pratyush Kumar, Sarvam AI’s co-founder, points out that in 2001, the idea that India could build digital infrastructure for a billion people would have sounded like a distant aspiration.
Few countries had attempted anything like it.
“What emerged over the next two decades was an unusual consequence, with the state building the foundation on which private enterprise could build at scale,” he says.

Sumant Sinha, who calls his renewable energy firm ReNew “a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision”, says the sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Modi has brought have changed the feel of India.
The biggest change, for him, is not any individual programme but that prosperity feels more widely distributed.
“Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did,” says Sinha.
Of course, the job is far from done.
Suman Bery, economist and former vice chairman of Niti Aayog, the government’s think tank, says: “It would be fatal to assume that, despite the past record, a steady 6 percent growth is assured.

It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible.” In his view, policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital.
Shah of Mahindra says the India of 2001 had aspiration and the India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability.

“The India of 2047,” he says, “must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.” Bhattacharya of Salesforce says the next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
“But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.”

stories.headline: US missions in West Asia issue security alert over possible Iran-backed attacks
stories.title: US missions in West Asia issue security alert over possible Iran-backed attacks
stories.summary: Jerusalem, Oct 19: US missions across West Asia posted a security alert on Sunday advising their nationals to “exercise heightened vigilance,” citing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and the potential for Iran and its allied groups to launch attacks against American interests. “Be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” the advisory said, adding that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.” “Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions,” the advisory said. The advisory came amid heightened security concerns in the region following drone and missile attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including a deadly strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 that killed 13 people, including an Indian national. The US views the Houthis as a key Iranian-backed armed group within Tehran’s regional network, with Iran providing weapons, funding and training, although the rebels retain considerable operational autonomy. US citizens travelling to or from West Asia were told to monitor information about airport and airline operations and develop contingency plans in advance. In view of the prevailing situation, the US embassy in Jerusalem also issued a list of “actions to be taken” and possible emergency assistance available. Fighting in Yemen has sharply escalated in October following the collapse of a multi-year informal cease-fire, with the Houthis launching major cross-border drone and missile strikes deep into Saudi Arabia. Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognised government to relocate to Aden. Saudi Arabia led a military coalition into Yemen in March 2015 to support the government and push back against the Houthis, triggering years of fighting and airstrikes. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 brought a period of relative calm, followed by Saudi-Houthi talks aimed at securing a lasting settlement. However, the ceasefire was never formalised into a comprehensive peace agreement. The renewed Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia adds a new regional dimension to the ongoing US-Iran conflict, threatening to widen hostilities beyond the immediate confrontation between Washington and Tehran. The conflict between the US and Iran, which started in February, remains locked in a military and diplomatic stalemate following the collapse of a June agreement. Iran continues to restrict shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the US maintains its naval port blockade on Tehran.

article_sentences: India and the US are close to finalising the trade deal but the entire process involves a complex set of factors that are required to be taken into account, said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ahead of his trip to India.
Rubio, who is in Uzbekistan now, will arrive in India on October 20.
He will meet External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar.
“We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now.
We're very close to doing that,” he told reporters on Monday.
He said the US has had to waive sanctions over the past few months because of the impact on global supplies and prices and the impact on other countries.
He said prices are high in the US but are “really, really high in a bunch of other countries”.
“We have to manage all of these things…Every country has a complex set of factors that it has to take into account.
Geography is real.
For some countries, it's very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources.
That's not an excuse, but all of that has to be balanced when making foreign policy,” he said.

The foreign policy of the US, of course, takes into account the war between Russia and Ukraine but it is not solely dominated by that, it has to take into account a variety of factors including its bilateral relationships with other countries and what they are realistically capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies, said Rubio.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court granted Nidhi Nehra Sharma anticipatory bail in a cheating case.

The Supreme Court has granted anticipatory bail to a woman accused in a cheating case after noting that she was cooperating with the investigation, news agency Press Trust of India reported on October 19.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran granted the relief to Nidhi Nehra Sharma in a case registered at Vasant Kunj North.
Police Station under Sections 420, 468, 471 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
Sharma is accused of fraudulently inducing a man to transfer substantial amounts on the false pretext of settling a company's liabilities.
She is also accused of diverting the money for personal benefit and deceiving the complainant by presenting an allegedly forged document.

“In the facts and circumstances of this case and considering submissions of the petitioner's counsel, we are of the opinion that the material against the petitioner falls short of the threshold required for refusal of anticipatory bail,” the bench said, according to PTI.

“Therefore, we order that in the event of arrest of the petitioner in connection with the offence enumerated above, she shall be released on bail, subject to terms and conditions that the Investigating Officer may deem fit to impose,” it added.
Advocate Ashwani Dubey, appearing for Sharma, submitted that she was cooperating with the investigation.
The court directed Sharma to appear before the court concerned after her release on bail, furnish fresh bail bonds and ensure her appearance during the trial.
The bench said the state could seek cancellation of the anticipatory bail if Sharma failed to follow its directions.

The Supreme Court has stayed the execution of the death sentence awarded to Indian Mujahideen operative Mohammad Tanvir for his role in the 2008 Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts, which killed 56 people, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh agreed to hear Tanvir's plea challenging the Gujarat High Court's July 7 verdict, which upheld the death sentences of 38 convicts in the case.
On July 26, 2008, 21 bombs exploded across Ahmedabad within 70 minutes, killing 56 people and injuring more than 200.
"There shall be stay of execution of the death sentence awarded to the appellant (Tanvir)," the Supreme Court said in its October 9 order, according to PTI.
The court ordered that the original case records be obtained from the trial court and the Gujarat High Court.
It also directed the Gujarat government to submit all probation officers' reports relating to Tanvir within eight weeks.
The superintendent of the jail concerned was asked to submit a report within eight weeks on the work performed by Tanvir in prison and his conduct and behaviour.
"The superintendent of prison of the concerned prison shall also get done the psychological evaluation of the appellant from the government medical hospital," the bench said.
The evaluation report must also be submitted within eight weeks.
The Supreme Court posted the matter for hearing after 12 weeks.
On October 1, it had stayed the execution of the death sentence awarded to Ahmed Bawa, also known as Abbu Abubakar Barelvi, another convict in the case.

body: A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh agreed to hear Tanvir's plea challenging the Gujarat High Court's July 7 verdict, which upheld the death sentences of 38 convicts in the case.
On July 26, 2008, 21 bombs exploded across Ahmedabad within 70 minutes, killing 56 people and injuring more than 200.
"There shall be stay of execution of the death sentence awarded to the appellant (Tanvir)," the Supreme Court said in its October 9 order, according to PTI.
The court ordered that the original case records be obtained from the trial court and the Gujarat High Court.
It also directed the Gujarat government to submit all probation officers' reports relating to Tanvir within eight weeks.
The superintendent of the jail concerned was asked to submit a report within eight weeks on the work performed by Tanvir in prison and his conduct and behaviour.
"The superintendent of prison of the concerned prison shall also get done the psychological evaluation of the appellant from the government medical hospital," the bench said.
The evaluation report must also be submitted within eight weeks.

stories.summary: 01 / THE BOTTLENECK What Are The Key Challenges In India’s Solar Market? Most seasoned industry leaders said that while India is making progressive strides towards adopting solar power, several bottlenecks continue to hinder its growth. Going forward, the biggest challenge will be to integrate growing solar into the grid, and to match it with demand profiles, which peaks during non-solar hours. This will require extensive planning, significant investment in expanding and modernizing grid infrastructure, and in supporting growth of energy storage to enable “peak shifting”. So, between now and 2030, we think the challenge is less about adding more gigawatts, and more about grid integration. Srivatsan Iyer, Global CEO, Hero Future Energies ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration rises, the challenge is that incremental generation is concentrated in the same daylight hours. The issue therefore shifts from the cost of producing a unit of solar electricity to its value to the grid at the time it is produced. We have already seen this globally through curtailment, low or even negative prices during high renewable hours and increasing evening flexibility requirements and these scenarios are emerging in India too. Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India’s renewable-energy sector is entering a period of very strong growth and is among the most remarkable story globally. Demand is expanding rapidly, particularly from commercial and industrial customers and from new areas such as data centres and AI infrastructure. The opportunity for solar and hybrid renewable energy is therefore very significant. The next phase will be about managing that growth effectively – ensuring that generation, infrastructure, technology and storage evolve together with rising demand. Kuldeep Jain, Founder & MD, Cleanmax ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Module capacity has moved well ahead of cell capacity, and cells are well ahead of wafers and ingots, which are still largely imported. As ALMM List-II for cells comes into effect, with a limited transition window for certain projects, the real test is whether domestic cell capacity can keep pace with module demand. A sector that assembles at home but depends on others for its core components has not yet secured its energy sovereignty. Closing that gap, cells first and then wafers and ingots, is the biggest task between now and 2030. Sohan Lal Agarwal, CMD, Websol Energy System Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In some regions, renewable capacity is growing faster than transmission and evacuation infrastructure, leading to grid congestion, curtailment and project delays. Ensuring that transmission and grid infrastructure keeps pace with generation will therefore be critical to fully utilising the renewable capacity India is adding. The biggest challenge will be moving from adding solar capacity to integrating it. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD and CEO, TrueRE Orion Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Transmission delays, curtailment risks in resource-rich states and the gap between when the sun shines and when India actually needs power are the real constraints. Closely tied to this is the financial health of distribution companies. Developers can only scale with confidence if offtake is reliable and payments are timely. And we cannot ignore supply-chain dependence. Reducing reliance on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon is essential for long-term resilience. Harsan Patel, Whole Time Director, KPI Green Energy 02 / THE STORAGE QUESTION Solar and storage: how soon is the marriage inevitable? There is an agreement that storage will play an important role. Speakers highlighted that solar power and BESS are gradually becoming inseparable, with their integration expected to become more prominent. When we began building solar plants, the conversation was only about megawatts and tariffs. Today, every serious discussion we have with a DISCOM or a large customer comes back to one question: Can you give us power when we actually need it? Solar alone cannot answer that question. Solar with storage can. We see this in our own portfolio. Just a few years ago, storage was treated as an experiment. Today it is part of the project everyone asks about first. Venugopal Rao Maddireddy, CMD, Pace Digitek Ltd ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rooftop solar and batteries are expected to converge in India over the next decade, shifting from an optional add-on to a standard configuration, led by commercial and industrial consumers. There are several reasons why the rooftop solar plus storage market is poised to grow. Time-of-day tariffs, which have been introduced for a larger number of consumers in several states, change more during peak hours of electricity use, such as the evening. Pawan Garg, CMD, Fujiyama ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration rises, managing intermittency, transmission, land, curtailment and evening peak demand will become increasingly important. India’s electricity demand is also rising at night, particularly due to cooling, while solar generation falls after sunset. The sector therefore needs to focus not just on adding GW, but on evacuation infrastructure, storage, forecasting and system flexibility. Gautam Mohanka, Director, Gautam Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every new solar tender now carries a minimum two-hour storage requirement at 10% of capacity. SECI’s latest FDRE tender is 1,200 MW with 4,800 MWh BESS attached. Such bids will be standard practice now. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building. Without grid expansion and large-scale BESS, we are forcing assets to sit idle and bleed revenue. Sanjeev Agarwal, Founder and Chairman, Hexa Climate ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The market is shifting from simply buying low-cost renewable power to asking for firm, peak-hour and more reliable supply. That naturally increases the role of storage. For commercial and industrial users, adoption will depend on battery costs, tariff structures and the value of backup and peak-demand management. Residential adoption is likely to be more selective for some time, depending on local economics and reliability needs. Ishver Dholakia, Founder & MD, Goldi Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The CEA has proposed that new ground-mounted solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 include co-located storage. Firm-power tenders already demand four hours of storage. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. Raju Komaravolu, CEO, Energy & Capital Goods (India), Zetwerk ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration increases, four things will decide success: strengthening transmission and power evacuation, adding battery storage and forecasting for grid flexibility, speeding up land acquisition and connectivity approvals, and reducing financing costs and regulatory uncertainty. We also need deeper domestic manufacturing beyond module assembly for long-term energy security. Col Pravir Mishra, COO, Insolare Energy Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- With domestic cell requirements taking effect from June 2026, strengthening the upstream ecosystem is critical. Wafers and ingots still remain largely import-dependent, underlining the need to deepen domestic manufacturing across the value chain. The second challenge is transmission, taking operational capacity to approximately 8.5 GW, while solar-plus-four-hour-storage tariffs have fallen to ₹2.70–2.76 per kWh. Policy support through viability-gap funding is also helping accelerate adoption. Ankit Singhania, Director, Navitas Solar 03 / THE GROWTH DRIVER What are the next big drivers of solar growth? Industry leaders also shared their views on the potential drivers of growth in India’s solar market. These included agrivoltaics, floating solar, and other emerging solar applications. Beyond conventional utility-scale and rooftop solar, major growth drivers for India include solar-plus-storage, data-centre power demand in the commercial and industrial segment, and new applications such as floating solar and agrivoltaics. Green hydrogen also has significant long-term potential, particularly for industries such as steel, refining and fertilisers, but its growth will depend on achieving commercially viable production costs. Harendra Tomar, Leader – Business Development, Sungrow ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration increases, the industry will also have to address land availability, project execution, financing and regulatory timelines more efficiently. These are not challenges for developers alone; they require coordination across the entire energy ecosystem. I believe the period to 2030 will mark a shift from capacity-led growth to system-led growth. The winners of the next phase will be those who can look beyond the solar plant itself and understand the complete journey of power—from generation to transmission, storage and consumption. Ravi Patel, Director – Sales & Marketing, Knack Energy ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India’s next phase of solar growth will be shaped by emerging technologies such as floating solar, agrivoltaics and green hydrogen, supported by battery energy storage systems (BESS) and grid modernisation. Generating more solar power is only part of the story. The larger task is making that power reliable, flexible and available when it is needed. We see agrivoltaics as a promising way to expand solar capacity. Simarpreet Singh, Executive Director and CEO, Hartek Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- One of the key constraints today is the availability of suitable land and adequate evacuation infrastructure for large-scale projects. In this context, alternative models such as floating solar and agrivoltaics are poised to gain traction in the near term. Among these, agrivoltaics holds particular promise, as it enables dual use of land—supporting both agriculture and energy generation. With the right policy incentives and regulatory support, agrivoltaics could emerge as a highly efficient and scalable solution for India’s next phase of solar growth. Tanmoy Duari, Axitec Energy India Pvt. Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India has 140M farmers. Agrivoltaics (solar + farming on same land) solves land conflict. PM KUSUM already is targeting 34 GW. With elevated structures, farmer earns Rs 40k/acre from solar + crop income. This is bankable because farmer gets dual income, and you get land without acquisition headache. Gujarat & Maharashtra are already financing at scale. India has 18,000 sq km of reservoirs. No land cost, 10% higher yield due to cooling are added benefits. Vikass Agarwwal, Founder & CEO, DebtBridge ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We see the next growth coming from solar that fits into everyday life and from new applications creating demand for clean electricity. Distributed solar added about 16.3 GW in FY26, over a third of the year's additions. Floating solar is a good example of thinking ahead. India has only about 700 MW today, against a NISE potential of around 102 GW. The new PM Surya Sarovar Yojana backs 5,000 MW with 10,000 MWh of storage, and it uses water bodies instead of competing for land. Rajesh Kaushal, EIS Business Group Head (India & SAARC), Delta Electronics India ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So far, lower power cost was the driver but from here on, decarbonization, green economy and net zero will be the bigger drivers of Solar energy growth in next decade. The government has mandated that minimum 10% of the storage is required so definitely storage and Solar will go together. Eventually if we consider NET ZERO targets we need to store maximum solar energy into the battery and use them during non-solar hour. Bharat Chhittarkka, Managing Director, Trex Energy ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The one thing people underestimate is commercial and industrial demand. Green open access rules have been eased, and companies now have R100 targets and export customers to answer to, especially with CBAM in force in Europe. Clean power is becoming a procurement requirement for Indian industry, not a CSR line. On the residential side, PM Surya Ghar has taken rooftop solar into tier-2 and tier-3 towns. Together, distributed solar is turning into a large market in its own right. Deepak Jain, CTO, INA Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Green hydrogen, floating solar and agrivoltaics each have strong potential. Green hydrogen can help industries cut emissions. Floating solar makes use of water bodies, and agrivoltaics allows farming and power generation on the same land. What they share is that they all extend solar beyond the traditional rooftop and ground-mounted plant. We believe the next phase of growth will come from solar combined with storage and tailored to specific needs, such as industrial power, land-constrained areas and farming communities. How fast each one grows will depend on falling costs, supportive policy and successful pilot projects. Sunsure Energy 04 / A SNEAK PEEK INTO THE FUTURE Where is the solar market heading to? Several industry leaders also offered a glimpse into the future of India’s solar market, drawing on past learnings, evolving policies, emerging trends, and other key developments shaping the sector. More tenders now require solar with storage, round-the-clock supply or firm power. What we’re still waiting for is the economics and the market rules to catch up so this can accelerate. The government is helping. Phase III of the Green Energy Corridor has just been approved, at Rs 1.86 lakh crore, and it should help move up to 135 GW of renewable power and add 50 GWh of battery storage. Srivatsan Iyer, Global CEO, Hero Future Energies ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Standalone solar will continue to make economic sense where daytime demand exists or the grid can absorb the generation. But as more solar enters the same daytime window, simply adding generation does not solve the larger power system requirement. The next unit of renewable capacity increasingly must solve for when power is required, not merely how much can be generated. Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In my view, storage becomes inseparable from utility-scale solar by regulation around 2027–28, and from C&I solar by economics in the states that move first. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. Raju Komaravolu, CEO, Energy & Capital Goods (India), Zetwerk ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- By 2030, I do not expect storage to be standard across every solar project. However, I do expect it to become a much more important part of how solar is planned and valued, especially since a significant amount of energy generated today is going unused or being wasted. The conversation will gradually shift from how cheaply solar can generate power to when that power can be delivered and how reliably it can meet demand. Ishver Dholakia, MD, Goldi Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The economics have also turned decisively. When Madhya Pradesh can secure solar-plus-storage power at a record-low Rs 2.70 per unit, the argument that storage is too expensive is simply over. Regulators have noticed too. Maharashtra now requires battery storage with new rooftop solar above 100 kW, and we expect other states to follow sooner than people think. Venugopal Rao Maddireddy, CMD, Pace Digitek Ltd ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Beyond generation, the convergence of solar with green hydrogen, green ammonia, data centres and other energy-intensive applications is creating entirely new consumption models. This broader convergence is reflected in our SCALE strategy, where we are leveraging technology, AI and partnerships and expanding into emerging clean-energy applications and new forms of energy consumption. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD & CEO, TrueRE Orion Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Buyers want reliable, round-the-clock supply, and the best answer will vary by region, resource and load profile. Wind-solar hybrid, and batteries will each have a role, and many projects will combine them. We serve round-the-clock needs today through wind-solar hybrid solutions, which complement storage. We expect this integrated approach to become the norm for new large-scale and commercial and industrial projects over the next four to five years. Kuldeep Jain, Founder and MD, CleanMax ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- But the real driver is on the demand side, not the supply side. Data centres. Companies like Google, Microsoft and Amazon are buying firm clean power at a scale that changes what we build, and they will not sign a contract that looks green on paper while drawing coal after sunset. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building. Sanjeev Agarwal, Founder and Chairman, Hexa Climate

stories.summary: The Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (HERC) has granted Eleven Power Private Limited a 25-year parallel electricity distribution licence for Gurugram and Nuh, allowing consumers in the two districts to choose between the company and the existing distribution licensee as its network expands. The licence, granted through an order under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003, marks the first parallel distribution licence in Haryana, according to the company. Eleven Power said the licence covers more than 8.3 lakh electricity consumers across residential, agricultural, commercial and industrial categories. The grant introduces the prospect of competition in electricity distribution in the two districts, although consumers will be able to switch only as Eleven Power’s network reaches their respective areas. The existing distribution licensee will continue to supply its consumers, and no immediate action is required from them, the company said. Section 14 of the Electricity Act permits more than one distribution licensee to operate in the same area, subject to the applicable regulatory framework. The model has been used in parts of India, including Mumbai. ₹4,717 crore investment planned over five years Eleven Power has proposed a capital investment of ₹4,717 crore over five years, from FY27 to FY31, to develop its distribution network across the licensed area. The company plans to begin supplying consumers from FY28, with the rollout to be undertaken in phases across five divisions: Gurugram Sub-urban, Gurugram City, Manesar, Sohna and Nuh. According to the company, the proposed network will use an N-1 redundancy design, a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)-enabled high-tension network, a distribution management system and ring-main configuration. The plan envisages underground cabling in Gurugram district and a combination of underground and overhead infrastructure in Nuh. The proposed consumer-facing systems include smart meters, digital billing and customer relationship centres. Eleven Power has said it intends to focus on supply reliability, transparent billing and grievance redressal. Within 60 days of the order, the company will submit a detailed implementation plan for the first phase and a protocol for consumers who opt to switch distributors, as specified in its announcement. Renewable energy to account for 80% of proposed power procurement Eleven Power has proposed sourcing 80% of its electricity from renewable energy, including through firm and dispatchable renewable energy contracts and the Green Day Ahead Market. A portion of the renewable power is expected to be sourced from within Haryana. The remaining 20% is proposed to come from thermal sources to support base-load requirements. The company has committed to supplying electricity on a non-discriminatory basis to all consumer categories and providing new connections within the timelines prescribed under the applicable HERC Electricity Supply Code, subject to the relevant requirements. Rising demand in Gurugram and Nuh The proposed licence area includes Gurugram, Manesar, Sohna and Nuh, where electricity demand is expected to increase alongside residential, commercial and industrial activity. According to projections cited in Eleven Power’s petition, based on growth rates approved by the commission, annual electricity sales in the licensed area are expected to rise from approximately 12,220 million units in FY25 to 18,224 million units in FY31. The company’s announcement also cited nearly 1.3 lakh pending applications for new connections and load enhancement across Haryana, involving more than 2,400 MW of load, as of October 2025. These figures provide context for the proposed investment, although they relate to the state as a whole rather than exclusively to Gurugram and Nuh. Commenting on the licence, Sunil Sachdeva, chairman of Eleven, said the company would focus on reliable electricity supply, timely new connections and procurement predominantly from renewable sources. The licence establishes a regulatory pathway for a second distribution utility in Gurugram and Nuh. The extent to which consumers exercise their choice will depend on the phased development of Eleven Power’s network, the availability of supply in individual areas and the applicable switching procedures. Tariffs will remain subject to regulation by HERC.

stories.headline: IMD update: Heavy rain outlook for Kerala, South Interior Karnataka retained
stories.title: IMD update: Heavy rain outlook for Kerala, South Interior Karnataka retained
stories.summary: An incoming circulation from Gulf of Thailand will be closely watched as it moves westwards towards the Andaman Sea, where it could likely develop into a low-pressure area and intensify
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Isolated heavy rainfall is likely over Kerala and Mahe for six days, South Interior Karnataka for five days, and Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and Rayalaseema for three days from Monday as the rain belt shifts to Kerala and Karnataka as the week progresses.
Lakshadweep may receive isolated heavy rainfall for three days from Wednesday, followed by another spell over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal for three days from Thursday.

The most recognisable city names that come under the meteorological subdivision of South Interior Karnataka are Bengaluru, Mysuru, Tumakuru, Mandya, Hassan, Shivamogga, Chikkamagaluru, Chitradurga, Davanagere and Kolar though weather for individual cities may vary from each other.
It was partly cloudy over Bengaluru at 10.30 am with chances of thundershowers less for most part of the day today (Monday).
The outlook for Chennai for today (Monday) is sun and showers, with rain prospects deteriorating untill midnight.

Probability for rain is at a high of 44 per cent at 11 am, which will progressively decline to 23 per cent by 6 pm, before improving with no break-out scenarios, according to an outlook from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
Rain footprint will shift from north and north-east of the city to west and west-southwest before briefly clearing up by 8 pm.

Clouds and precipitation will likely be focused over an area bounded by Pulicat Lake to Chennai and adjoining coast as well as parts of Puducherry and then west-northwest towards Salem, Tiruchirappalli, parts of Dindigul, Madurai and Thoothukudi with parts of Delta districts also seen making some gains during the day.

An IMD assessment in the morning said the current weather pattern is being sustained by an upper-air cyclonic circulation over the south-west Bay of Bengal and adjoining north Tamil Nadu coast, with a trough extending towards the north-west Bay.
As of today (Monday), other cyclonic circulations persist over North Interior Karnataka, the Gulf of Thailand, and south-east Bangladesh and Tripura.
The incoming circulation from the Gulf of Thailand will be closely watched as it moves westwards towards the Andaman Sea, where it could likely develop into a low-pressure area and intensify.
The IMD broadly shares this outlook, pointing to the possibility of a new rain-bearing system emerging over the Bay of Bengal.

stories.headline: Odisha Issues Consultancy Tender for 225 MW Floating Solar + BESS Project
stories.title: Odisha Issues Consultancy Tender for 225 MW Floating Solar + BESS Project
stories.summary: Grid Corporation of Odisha (GRIDCO), a state owned PSU and the nodal agency has sought bids for undertaking an impact study for developing floating solar projects across the states, seeking Expression of Interests ( EoIs) till November 17, 2026 Through this tender, the developers are required to select solar developers to develop, operate and maintain three units of grid-connected floating solar photovoltaic (FSPV) projects of 75 MW each, collectively, aggregating to 225 MW. Combined with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), together this project aims to supply power to GRIDCO . GRIDCO through the latest consultancy tender requires the bidders to act as the solar park developer for developing solar park over the Upper Indravati reservoir (Upper Indravati Solar Park) under its renewable energy Renewable Energy Policy. Scope of Work Under the scope of work, the developer is expected to undertake the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) , and prepare E&S with IFC's Environmental and Social Performance Standards (2012). The deliverables include the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA), Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP), Occupational Health Safety (OHS) plan and associated management instruments including the Livelihood Restoration Plan (LRP), Indigenous Peoples Development Plan (IPDP), Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP), and Grievance Mechanism (GM). A Livelihood Restoration Framework (LRF) and Stakeholder Engagement Framework (SEF) have been prepared at the scoping stage. The ESIA Consultant would be based on detailed impact assessment and identification of affected persons, prepare a Livelihood Restoration Plan (LRP) as part of the ESIA/ESMP documentation in accordance with the LRF Project Components Footprint The core AOI includes all areas directly occupied or physically disturbed by the Project components and associated facilities: The Floating Solar Photovoltaic ( FSPV ) project would be installed over the Indravati Reservoir (~6.5 sq. km) with a 33 kV transmission line and associated buffer. Launching pad, temporary storage areas. The developer would also have to build a Power Substation (PSS), Right of Way ( RoW ) for the 220 kV transmission line up to Mukhiguda Grid Substation. The Reservoir area within Floating solar project area, where direct aquatic ecological impacts are anticipated. The scope of work covers 15 villages comprising of 8 project villages and 7 AoI villages) These areas are anticipated to experience direct environmental and social interactions associated with the Project. Project footprint included within the following villages. The floating solar project is at Padepadar, Gaura Kurumuli and Paraja Kurumuli. The transmission Line would connect Padepadar, Uparchobari, Podapadar, Tikilipadar, Mahulpatna, Kamaridhi Scope of the Study: The developer is required ti review all existing project information and establish a baseline for climate and hydrological conditions. This includes an initial narrative review of all available documents and datasets to understand the project context, technical design considerations, and reservoir-dam operating environment. The following key documents and datasets will be collected and reviewed. The Project design reports and layout plans. It would be required to manage Bathymetry data, reservoir characteristics, and dam technical information and also develop Hydrological studies prepared as part of the project’s technical design.
